        Directions (Q.1-Q.24): Read the passage carefully and answer the questions.
        Passage (Q.1-Q.5): The expansion of cooperative banking brought an uneven but unmistakable shift in rural
        finance across many districts. In its early years, it gained momentum among small cultivators, artisans, and petty
        traders who had long relied on moneylenders for immediate relief. Organizers moved from settlement to
        settlement, holding meetings, praising thrift, and urging households to place even the smallest surplus into a
        common fund. In a surprisingly short time, local credit societies began to appear in pockets where formal banking
        had earlier left almost no trace.
        The movement revealed that financial organization was not the preserve of cities or of those already secure in
        wealth. Its influence among villagers, self-help groups, and local workers was visible, though not evenly
        distributed. Some regions accepted the idea with enthusiasm, while others remained only partly touched by it.
        The most striking feature was the willingness of people who had never participated in institutional finance to
        trust a shared pool of money and to treat saving as a collective discipline rather than a private habit.
        Women’s participation in many societies further altered the movement’s character. In several places, it gave the
        societies a steadier, more durable form. It would be difficult to deny that this wider participation, more than any
        single organizer’s appeal, supplied the movement with its genuine mass base in many districts. It was therefore
        unfortunate that the early cooperative spirit did not remain equally strong in later years, when local rivalries,
        suspicion, and factional splits began to weaken the very societies that had once seemed so promising.

Passage (Q.6-Q.10): There were languages long before there was writing. The earliest human communities
        spoke, argued, named their surroundings, and transmitted knowledge across generations through sound alone.
        Yet none of this left a direct trace. The spoken word vanished as soon as it was uttered, and the humans who
        used it had no expectation that their voices would one day be studied, reconstructed, or even remembered. In this
        sense, prehistoric language was as invisible to the future as the footprints of animals washed away by rain.
        Linguists who study the origins of language face a peculiar difficulty: they must reconstruct a phenomenon that
        leaves no fossil record. Bones, tools, and cave paintings survive; spoken words do not. The discipline has
        therefore had to work indirectly, drawing on comparative studies of living languages, the anatomy of ancient
        skulls, and the behaviour of non-human primates. Some researchers have argued that the presence of a descended
        larynx in ancient human skulls is evidence of speech; others have cautioned that anatomy alone cannot confirm
        whether a creature actually used language or merely had the physical capacity to do so.
        The distinction matters because capacity is not the same as use. A parrot can reproduce human sounds with
        striking accuracy, yet nobody seriously claims that parrots possess language in the way humans do. What
        separates human language from animal communication is not the ability to make sounds, but the ability to
        combine symbols in an open-ended way, generating sentences that have never been spoken before and conveying
        meanings that go far beyond immediate experience. This generative property is what allowed humans to speak
        of things that do not exist, to plan for futures that have not yet arrived, and to build the elaborate collective
        fictions gods, nations, money upon which all complex societies depend.
        (Extracted, with edits and revisions, from a scholarly essay on the evolutionary origins of human language)

questions.stimulus:
Passage (Q.6-Q.10): There were languages long before there was writing. The earliest human communities
        spoke, argued, named their surroundings, and transmitted knowledge across generations through sound alone.
        Yet none of this left a direct trace. The spoken word vanished as soon as it was uttered, and the humans who
        used it had no expectation that their voices would one day be studied, reconstructed, or even remembered. In this
        sense, prehistoric language was as invisible to the future as the footprints of animals washed away by rain.
        Linguists who study the origins of language face a peculiar difficulty: they must reconstruct a phenomenon that
        leaves no fossil record. Bones, tools, and cave paintings survive; spoken words do not. The discipline has
        therefore had to work indirectly, drawing on comparative studies of living languages, the anatomy of ancient
        skulls, and the behaviour of non-human primates. Some researchers have argued that the presence of a descended
        larynx in ancient human skulls is evidence of speech; others have cautioned that anatomy alone cannot confirm
        whether a creature actually used language or merely had the physical capacity to do so.
        The distinction matters because capacity is not the same as use. A parrot can reproduce human sounds with
        striking accuracy, yet nobody seriously claims that parrots possess language in the way humans do. What
        separates human language from animal communication is not the ability to make sounds, but the ability to
        combine symbols in an open-ended way, generating sentences that have never been spoken before and conveying
        meanings that go far beyond immediate experience. This generative property is what allowed humans to speak
        of things that do not exist, to plan for futures that have not yet arrived, and to build the elaborate collective
        fictions gods, nations, money upon which all complex societies depend.
        (Extracted, with edits and revisions, from a scholarly essay on the evolutionary origins of human language)

questions.stimulus:
Passage (Q.11-Q.15): In 1985, only a minority of the world’s states were rated as broadly democratic by
        international observers, yet within a generation the political map of several continents had altered sharply.
        Competitive elections, constitutional governments, and expanded civil liberties spread across regions that had
        long been ruled by military commanders or single-party systems. This period is often described as a democratic
        tide; for many analysts, it was not merely a change in rulers but a change in political expectations. Ordinary
        citizens increasingly came to assume that governments should be answerable, elections should matter, and power
        should be open to contest.
        Behind this shift lay a deeper social movement. The expansion of schooling made larger populations literate in
        politics as well as in language. New communication networks carried images, slogans, and grievances across
        borders with unusual speed. Cheaper travel allowed discontented citizens to relocate, compare regimes, or exit
        states that seemed intolerable. Rising incomes also mattered, because prosperity tends to sharpen demands for
        dignity, legal protection, and a larger voice in public life. Taken together, these forces turned once-passive
        populations into active participants in political change.
        Yet the tide did not keep rising indefinitely. By the second decade of the twenty-first century, observers began
        speaking of democratic fatigue. In a number of countries that had once seemed securely transformed, electoral
        procedures remained in place while institutions lost credibility, public trust thinned, and executive power
        accumulated in fewer hands. The new danger was not always outright dictatorship; sometimes it was democratic
        form without democratic substance. The decline was gradual enough to escape notice at first, but broad enough
        to suggest that political openings can narrow even without dramatic collapse.

questions.stimulus:
Passage (Q.16-Q.20): My cousin and I were returning by the evening train after a marriage feast when we found
        ourselves beside a gentleman of singular composure. His coat was plain to the point of anonymity, yet his speech
        carried the confidence of a man who had long ago settled every controversy to his own satisfaction. At first, we
        judged him by his appearance and thought him provincial; within minutes, we had begun to suspect that our
        judgment was provincial instead. He spoke of politics as though it were a family errand, of poetry as though it
        were arithmetic, and of the future as though he had already received its draft.

1


        We had, until then, lived in the comfortable belief that the world’s matters were arranged in neat compartments,
        one for officials, one for merchants, and one for newspapers. He dismantled that belief with a smile so mild that
        it nearly passed for courtesy. Russians, Englishmen, village notables, secret policy, and the machinery of public
        life all appeared in his remarks with the ease of objects kept in a drawer. My cousin, who had lately developed
        a fondness for spiritual matters, immediately concluded that such fluency could only arise from some occult
        adjustment of the soul. He began to look at each sentence as though it were a revelation and at each pause as
        though it concealed another.
        The gentleman seemed to enjoy this devotion without ever acknowledging it directly. If he noticed our
        amazement, he did not disturb it; if he was amused, he was amused with perfect politeness. By the time we
        reached the junction, it was nearly ten, and the delay announced by the station-master gave me hope of sleep. I
        spread my shawl on the bench and surrendered myself to rest. But the stranger, seeing that I had become
        momentarily defenseless, began a story with such calm assurance that the night, which had seemed to belong to
        me, was immediately taken over by his voice.

Passage (Q.21-Q.24): Man, unlike the rest of us, consumes without ever truly producing. He does not yield
        milk, he does not hatch eggs, he cannot draw the plough, and he is too slow to seize a rabbit. Yet he presumes to
        rule over all creatures, and by that presumption alone he claims the fruits of labour as his own. He gives us the
        minimum that will prevent collapse, while taking for himself the larger share that our bodies and fields have
        made possible. The soil is turned by our strength, the dung is returned to the earth by our labour, and still we
        remain no richer than the hides we were born with.
        Look at the cows: how much milk have they given this year, and where is it now? It was meant to feed calves,
        yet it has gone instead to those who stand above us. Look at the hens: how many eggs have they laid, and how
        many have ever become chicks? Most have been carried off to market, where they were turned into profit for


1


        others. And Clover, think of the foals she bore—each was taken away while still young, before it could return a
        single day of comfort. After all those years in the field and all those births, what did she keep except a ration and
        a stall?
        Even our lives, such as they are, are deliberately shortened. I complain least, for I am among the fortunate: twelve
        years old, and already mother to over four hundred piglets. That, they say, is the pig’s proper span. But no animal,
        whatever its species, is spared at the end. The young among you may imagine a long road ahead; in truth, the
        block waits for all of us. Boxer, once your strength weakens, Jones will sell you to the knacker; the knife will do
        the rest, and your body will be turned to use for others. The old dog, once faithful and now useless, is no better
        off: a brick and a pond are all that remain.

        university status through the AMU Act of 1920. Amendments in 1951 and 1965 restructured its governance,
        stripping its minority character. In Azeez Basha v. Union of India, the Supreme Court held that AMU was
        established through legislation and not by a minority community, denying it Article 30 protections. The 1981

        institutions: the foundational idea, purpose, contributions by the minority community, and administrative
        structure demonstrating autonomy for protecting minority interests. Minority institutions need not exclusively
        serve minorities or provide religious education but must be predominantly established for their benefit. Even
        administrating non-minority students does not alter the minority character of the institution on this particular
        basis. The Court overruled Azeez Basha, affirming that Article 30 protections apply equally to pre-Constitution
        institutions. The ruling emphasized that "establishment" refers to the efforts and intent of minority founders, not

        institutions while upholding constitutional protections for diversity in India.

Passage (Q.65-Q.68): There are two principal theories on the relationship between international law and
        domestic law- monism and dualism. Monism posits that international law and municipal law form part of a
        unified, singular legal order, meaning that international treaties become automatically enforceable within
        domestic territory upon ratification without requiring separate legislative translation. In contrast, India
        predominantly adopts a Dualist approach rooted in its post-colonial constitutional design. Under this framework,
        international conventions, treaties, or declarations signed by the executive branch do not automatically transform
        into enforceable domestic law. For an international instrument to possess binding statutory force over private
        citizens or municipal administrative machinery, the Union Parliament must actively internalize it through valid
        municipal legislation.
        The text of the Constitution of India meticulously distributes this foreign affairs power. Under Article 246 read
        with Entries 13 and 14 of List I (Union List) of the Seventh Schedule, the power to enter into treaties, agreements,
        and conventions with foreign nations rests exclusively with the Central Government. To give teeth to these

1


        commitments, Article 253 overrides ordinary federal distributions of power, granting Parliament the plenary
        authority to make any law for the whole or any part of the territory of India specifically for implementing an
        international treaty, agreement, or convention. Conversely, Article 51(c), situated within the Directive Principles
        of State Policy (DPSP), mandates that the State shall endeavor to "foster respect for international law and treaty
        obligations." Because it is a DPSP, Article 51(c) is textually non-enforceable before courts of law; it serves as a
        guiding light for governance rather than an independent source of enforceable individual rights.
        Despite India's formal dualist baseline, the Supreme Court of India has dynamically bridged the gap between
        municipal gaps and global human rights norms through evolutionary judicial interpretation. The judiciary has
        established a fundamental rule of construction: where domestic legislation is ambiguous, or where there exists a
        complete statutory vacuum on a crucial civil liberty issue, the courts will read international covenants—such as
        the International Covenant on Civil and Political Rights (ICCPR) or the Convention on the Elimination of All
        Forms of Discrimination against Women (CEDAW)—into the fundamental rights chapter under Part III.
        This interpretive synthesis operates under strict constitutional guardrails. First, international norms can only be
        used as interpretive aids to expand, clarify, or operationalize domestic principles like the right to life and dignity
        under Article 21; they cannot be used to introduce entirely alien structures that explicitly conflict with an existing,
        clear parliamentary statute. Second, if a direct, irreconcilable conflict emerges between an explicit domestic law
        and an international treaty commitment, the domestic municipal law binds the courts absolutely. Thus, the Indian
        judiciary employs international law not as a parallel source of independent sovereignty, but as a catalyst for
        creative internal statutory expansion.

Passage (Q.69-Q.72): ‘Coparcenary’ and ‘Hindu undivided family’ are not words we hear often, but they are
        the foundation of a discriminatory concept in Indian family law responsible for an annual revenue loss of
        thousands of crores to the Indian exchequer. In 1948, BR Ambedkar proposed its abolition on the basis that it
        was not in sync with the times. Legal experts have claimed that now, the Uttarakhand Uniform Civil Code finally
        abolishes these concepts. Closer examination reveals that it does not. Hindu joint families in northern and western
        India are governed by the ‘mitakshara’ school of law, which enables them to hold their ancestral property
        collectively. This property is managed by a sub-unit of the joint family called a ‘coparcenary’. Upon birth, each
        coparcener acquires a share in the common property (right by birth). When a coparcener dies, the property is
        partitioned and the deceased person’s share is separated. This share then passes as per the prescribed scheme of
        succession. It is based on the anachronistic concept of the jointness of food and worship in Hindu joint families
        and the moral obligation of certain members (traditionally males) to maintain and look after the whole family.
        Under the Hindu Succession Act (HSA) 1956, only males could be coparceners. The underlying principle was
        that only a son has a birthright in ancestral property — a prominent maxim of classical Hindu law. In 2005,
        Parliament amended the HSA to correct the gender imbalance within Hindu law by making daughters
        coparceners at par with sons. However, it did not abolish the coparcenary system and the right that sons (and
        now also daughters) acquire in their ancestral property upon their birth. Over the years, there have been calls for
        the abolition of the coparcenary system as it is not in alignment with modern family structures, something that
        was pointed out during the debates on the Hindu Code Bill itself. The UUCC maintains the status quo and does
        not abolish coparcenary property despite earlier indications. It merely defines a person’s ‘estate’ to include their
        share in the ancestral property; in other words, their coparcenary share. Once the property gets partitioned upon
        a coparcener’s death (as per the HSA), it will devolve to heirs based on the intestate succession scheme laid
        down in the UUCC. This is the case since the UUCC only provides that those parts of the HSA that are
        inconsistent with it will no longer apply in Uttarakhand. Thus, coparceners will continue to come into existence

Passage (Q.78-Q.82): In August 2023, a large-scale leakage of Chlorine gas was reported from the water-
        treatment chemical storage unit of “AquaPure Chemicals Ltd.” situated near the residential area of Nirmalpur
        city. The accident allegedly occurred when a corroded valve in one of the storage tanks was not replaced despite
        repeated internal maintenance warnings. During the night shift, pressure inside the tank increased, causing
        Chlorine gas to escape into the surrounding locality. Several workers complained of breathing difficulty, burning
        sensation in the eyes, and nausea, while residents of nearby colonies had to be evacuated. Chlorine is a hazardous
        chemical used in industrial and water-treatment processes, and its uncontrolled release can cause serious injury
        to human health and damage to the environment.
        Environmental law recognises certain important principles to determine liability in such cases. The Polluter
        Pays Principle requires the person or enterprise responsible for environmental damage to bear the cost of
        restoring the environment and compensating affected persons. It is not limited only to payment of money to
        individual victims but also extends to the cost of repairing environmental damage.
        The Principle of Strict Liability, laid down in Rylands v. Fletcher, applies where a person brings or keeps a
        hazardous substance on land for a non-natural use and that substance escapes and causes damage. However, this
        principle recognises certain exceptions, such as Act of God, act of a stranger, consent of the injured person,
        statutory authority, or fault of the injured person.

1


        The Principle of Absolute Liability, developed in M.C. Mehta v. Union of India, is stricter. When an enterprise
        is engaged in a hazardous or inherently dangerous activity and harm is caused, it has an absolute and non-
        delegable duty to compensate. It cannot escape liability by arguing that it was not negligent, that it took
        reasonable care, or that the harm was caused by circumstances which may operate as exceptions under strict
        liability. Therefore, enterprises dealing with hazardous substances may be held liable not only for direct injury
        to individuals but also for environmental harm resulting from their activities.
